pharm: Phenothiazine derivative that competitively blocks central and peripheral histamine H1 receptors; also exerts strong anticholinergic, sedative, and antiemetic actions with only weak dopamine-antagonist activity (about 1/10 that of chlorpromazine).
quick: Use only if benefit justifies fetal risk
Excretion unknown; weigh risk vs benefit
No specific adjustment; caution in elderly
summary: Promethazine is a sedating phenothiazine H1-antihistamine with antiemetic and sedative properties, used for allergy, nausea/vomiting, motion sickness, sedation, and as an adjunct to analgesics. It carries two boxed warnings: fatal respiratory depression in children under 2 years (contraindicated) and severe tissue injury/gangrene with intravenous use. Pronounced sedation, anticholinergic effects, EPS, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome may occur.
indications: Perennial and seasonal allergic rhinitis; vasomotor rhinitis
Allergic conjunctivitis from inhalant allergens and foods
Mild uncomplicated allergic skin reactions (urticaria, angioedema); dermographism
Amelioration of allergic reactions to blood or plasma; adjunct to epinephrine in anaphylaxis after acute control
Prevention and control of nausea and vomiting with anesthesia/surgery and postoperative
Active and prophylactic treatment of motion sickness
Preoperative, postoperative, and obstetric sedation; relief of apprehension and light sleep
Adjunct to meperidine or other analgesics for postoperative pain

dosage.d: 25 mg at bedtime; or 12.5 mg before meals and at bedtime; 6.25-12.5 mg three times daily may suffice
dosage.n: 25 mg controls minor allergic transfusion reactions

dosage.t: First dose 30-60 min before travel, repeat 8-12 h later; on later days 25 mg on rising and before evening meal

dosage.n: Children >=2 yr: 0.5 mg/lb; avoid in vomiting of unknown etiology

dosage.d: 50 mg night before surgery; 25-50 mg postoperative adjunct to analgesics
dosage.n: Children >=2 yr: 12.5-25 mg; reduce concomitant narcotic/barbiturate dose
Risk of fatal respiratory depression (boxed warning)

admin: Suppository formulation is for RECTAL administration only
Contraindicated in children under 2 years of age (fatal respiratory depression)
In children 2 years and older use the LOWEST effective dose and avoid other respiratory depressants
If injectable used, prefer deep IM; IV carries risk of severe tissue injury/gangrene from extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection
When combined with narcotics or barbiturates, reduce their dose (barbiturates by at least half; narcotics by one-quarter to one-half)
moa: Promethazine is a phenothiazine derivative whose branched side chain and lack of ring substitution give it potent H1-antihistaminic activity with relatively weak dopamine antagonism. By competitively blocking central and peripheral histamine H1 receptors it relieves allergic symptoms; central H1 and muscarinic blockade produce sedation and antiemetic/antimotion-sickness effects, partly via action on the vestibular system and chemoreceptor trigger zone.

absolute: Pediatric patients less than 2 years of age (potential for fatal respiratory depression - boxed warning)
Known hypersensitivity or idiosyncratic reaction to promethazine or other phenothiazines
Treatment of lower respiratory tract symptoms including asthma
relative: Seizure disorders or concurrent drugs that lower seizure threshold
Bone-marrow depression or concurrent marrow-toxic agents
Narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, bladder-neck obstruction, stenosing peptic ulcer, pyloroduodenal obstruction
Cardiovascular disease or hepatic impairment; elderly patients
Children with signs suggestive of Reye's syndrome or hepatic disease
monitor: Respiratory status, especially with other CNS/respiratory depressants
Level of sedation and mental/physical impairment
Signs of EPS (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, tongue protrusion) and NMS
CBC if marrow-toxic risk; involuntary muscle movements

preg: No adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Animal feeding studies (rat) did not demonstrate teratogenicity at 6.25-12.5 mg/kg. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Administration within two weeks of delivery may inhibit platelet aggregation in the newborn.
lact: It is not known whether promethazine is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, weighing the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is provided. Use cautiously in the elderly, who may have decreased renal, hepatic, or cardiac function and greater susceptibility to sedation and confusion.
hepatic: Use cautiously in patients with impaired liver function. Cholestatic jaundice has been associated with promethazine administration. Avoid in children whose presentation may suggest Reye's syndrome or other hepatic disease.

major: CNS depressants - alcohol, sedatives/hypnotics (barbiturates), narcotics/narcotic analgesics, general anesthetics, tricyclic antidepressants, tranquilizers (additive sedation and potentially fatal respiratory depression; reduce or avoid)
Epinephrine - do NOT use to treat promethazine-induced hypotension (promethazine can reverse epinephrine's pressor effect, paradoxically lowering BP)
Other respiratory depressants (additive risk of fatal respiratory depression, especially in children)
moderate: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (increased incidence of extrapyramidal effects)
Drugs that lower seizure threshold (narcotics, local anesthetics)
interactions.food: Not significantly affected; the suppository is administered rectally.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - alcohol markedly enhances CNS depression and impairment.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-negative or false-positive immunological pregnancy tests; may increase blood glucose (glucose tolerance test).

serious: Extrapyramidal symptoms (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, tongue protrusion, dystonia)
Severe tissue injury/gangrene with IV use
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperpyrexia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Respiratory rate and adequacy, especially in children >=2 yr and with concomitant CNS depressants
Degree of sedation and ability to perform hazardous tasks
Signs of EPS and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability)
CBC if bone-marrow depression risk; liver function if jaundice suspected
IV injection site for extravasation/tissue injury if injectable used
counsel: May cause marked drowsiness; avoid driving or operating machinery until effects are known
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives - they intensify drowsiness and breathing problems
Never give to children under 2 years; use the lowest dose with caution in older children
Report involuntary muscle movements, restlessness, or abnormal movements
Avoid prolonged sun exposure (photosensitivity); report severe injection-site pain or burning
pk: Effects develop over the first hours; sedation typically within ~1 hour
Generally 4-6 hours, may persist up to 12 hours
Suppositories: refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F); dispense in well-closed container
pearls: Two boxed warnings: (1) fatal respiratory depression in children <2 yr (contraindicated, not dose-related); (2) severe tissue injury including gangrene with IV use - prefer deep IM and never inject intra-arterially or subcutaneously
Naloxone does NOT reverse promethazine-induced respiratory/CNS depression
Do NOT use epinephrine for promethazine-associated hypotension - it can further lower blood pressure
Watch for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and extrapyramidal reactions despite weak dopamine antagonism
Antiemetic use is not recommended for uncomplicated vomiting in children; reserve for prolonged vomiting of known cause
missed: When used on a scheduled basis, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose; do not double up. As-needed doses are simply taken when symptoms recur within the labeled interval.
overdose: Ranges from mild CNS/cardiovascular depression to profound hypotension, respiratory depression, unconsciousness, and sudden death; atropine-like signs (dry mouth, dilated pupils, flushing), hyperreflexia, and rarely convulsions can occur, with paradoxical hyperexcitability in children. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: secure airway and assist ventilation, give activated charcoal, control seizures with diazepam, correct acidosis/electrolytes. For hypotension use IV fluids and, if needed, norepinephrine or phenylephrine - NOT epinephrine. Naloxone is ineffective; dialysis is not helpful.
